name: Bar Reverse Curl
variant: Standing pronated-grip curl using a straight bar or EZ/curl bar; wrist-extension curls and neutral-grip hammer curls are separate movements.
description: Stand tall holding the bar with a pronated grip, keep the wrists firm and the elbows near the ribs, curl upward without swinging, then lower under control until the elbows are long while keeping the forearms turned over.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful for brachioradialis and elbow-flexor accessory work, but less direct for biceps brachii hypertrophy than supinated curl variants.

strength.rationale: Builds local pronated-grip elbow-flexion strength, but absolute loads are usually modest.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can expose the wrist extensors, brachioradialis, and elbow to controlled pronated loading, but should be progressed conservatively.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Some grip and forearm relevance exists for pulling and grappling tasks, but the movement is still a narrow accessory.

control.rationale: Requires wrist-position discipline and anti-swing control, but little whole-body coordination.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Focused forearm and elbow-flexor stimulus with low systemic fatigue.

setup.rationale: Needs a suitable bar and enough wrist comfort with the pronated grip.

ease.rationale: Simple to perform, but the pronated grip can feel awkward and encourages wrist collapse if overloaded.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are trackable, though bar jumps and wrist comfort can limit progression.

support.rationale: No external support is provided; the user must stabilize the wrists, elbows, shoulders, and torso.

primary.name: Brachioradialis
primary.evidenceShort: Pronated curl handgrip EMG directly measures brachioradialis.
primary.evidence: Curl handgrip EMG directly measured brachioradialis activity during pronated curl conditions. The pronated grip reduces the biceps brachii supination advantage and shifts the visible target toward brachioradialis.

secondary.name: Brachialis
secondary.evidenceShort: Deep elbow flexor contribution is expected during pronated elbow flexion.
secondary.evidence: Brachialis is a major elbow flexor independent of forearm supination. It is included from anatomy and pronated-curl mechanics because the main surface EMG sources cannot isolate it cleanly.

secondary.name: Biceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Pronated curl EMG still shows biceps contribution.
secondary.evidence: Curl handgrip EMG measured biceps brachii activity during pronated curl conditions. It is secondary because pronation reduces the biceps brachii role compared with supinated curls.

support.name: Wrist extensors
support.evidenceShort: Pronated bar curls require wrist-extension support.
support.evidence: Forearm EMG evidence supports wrist extensor involvement in wrist-position control. They are listed as support because the user must resist wrist flexion while holding a pronated bar.

evidence.verdict: Bar reverse curl: brachioradialis primary; brachialis and biceps brachii secondary; wrist extensors support.
evidence.clinicalShort: Pronated curl evidence supports a forearm-biased elbow-flexion accessory; wrist tolerance is a key boundary.
evidence.limitsShort: Bar shape, wrist comfort, pronation angle, grip width, torso swing, load, tempo, and elbow drift can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The bar reverse curl is classified as a standing pronated-grip elbow-flexion accessory. Handgrip-specific curl EMG supports brachioradialis as the main visible target, with biceps brachii and brachialis as secondary elbow flexors. Wrist extensors are shown as support because the pronated bar requires active wrist-position control.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: This is a useful pull-day accessory when the user wants forearm and brachioradialis coverage that standard supinated curls may underdose. It should remain separate from wrist-extension curls because the primary joint action here is elbow flexion, not wrist extension.
evidence.limitations: Direct evidence is strongest for pronated curl handgrip conditions and general bar/EZ/dumbbell curl variants rather than one standardized EZ-bar reverse curl. Wrist discomfort can limit usefulness before the elbow flexors are fully challenged.

studies.finding: Supinated, pronated, and neutral cable curl handgrips changed biceps brachii, brachioradialis, and anterior deltoid excitation in competitive bodybuilders.
studies.citation: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Toninelli N, Padovan R, Esposito F, Ce E. Biceps Brachii and Brachioradialis Excitation in Biceps Curl Exercise: Different Handgrips, Different Synergy. Sports. 2023;11(3):64. doi:10.3390/sports11030064.
studies.relevance: Most direct handgrip evidence for pronated curl biceps brachii and brachioradialis contribution.

studies.finding: Straight barbell, EZ-bar, and dumbbell curls produced different biceps brachii and brachioradialis EMG patterns across repetition phases.
studies.citation: Marcolin G, Panizzolo FA, Petrone N, Moro T, Grigoletto D, Piccolo D, Paoli A. Differences in electromyographic activity of biceps brachii and brachioradialis while performing three variants of curl. PeerJ. 2018;6:e5165. doi:10.7717/peerj.5165.
studies.relevance: Bar and EZ-bar curl evidence for elbow-flexor recruitment and bar-shape boundaries.

studies.type: Forearm rotation and wrist muscle EMG
studies.shortCitation: Ikeda et al., J Orthop Surg Res, 2025
studies.finding: Wrist flexor and extensor activity changed with forearm rotation during controlled wrist torque tasks.
studies.citation: Ikeda K, Kaneoka K, Matsunaga N, Ikumi A, Yamazaki M, Yoshii Y. Effects of forearm rotation on wrist flexor and extensor muscle activities. Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery and Research. 2025;20(1):53. doi:10.1186/s13018-024-05363-x.
studies.relevance: Forearm and wrist-position evidence for wrist extensor support during pronated gripping.

studies.type: Forearm EMG during wrist and finger movements
studies.finding: Multi-channel EMG quantified forearm muscle activity during wrist and finger movement tasks.
studies.citation: Gazzoni M, Celadon N, Mastrapasqua D, Paleari M, Margaria V, Ariano P. Quantifying forearm muscle activity during wrist and finger movements by means of multi-channel electromyography. PLoS ONE. 2014;9(10):e109943. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0109943.
studies.relevance: Broader forearm EMG context for wrist-position stabilization.
